---
title: "Exceptions: when code cannot go on"
---

Since the calculator chapter, every project of yours opens with the same safety
line: look up an element, and `throw new Error(...)` when it is not there. You
have typed that `throw` a dozen times and never watched it fire. This chapter
fires it, and then teaches the other half of the story, where code further out
catches what a `throw` sends up.

## Break your own page {#sec-exceptions-experiment}

Create a new app `error-tour` from our template inside `coursework/`. Replace
`src/index.ts` with this:

```ts
const header = document.querySelector<HTMLHeadingElement>('#helloWorldHeader');
if (!header) {
  throw new Error('Element #helloWorldHeader not found');
}

header.textContent = 'Nothing broke';
console.log('the last line of the file');
```

Run `npm start`, open the page, and press F12 for the developer tools. The
heading says `Nothing broke` and the console says `the last line of the file`.

Now break it on purpose. In `index.html`, rename the heading's id from
`helloWorldHeader` to `pageHeader`, and save. The page reloads with the
heading back at `Hello World`, because the line that sets `textContent` never
ran. `the last line of the file` is gone from the console too. In its place
stands a red line with the message you wrote:

```
Uncaught Error: Element #helloWorldHeader not found
```

Under it sits the stack: the file and the line number where the `throw`
happened.

## What throw does to everything above it {#sec-exceptions-throw}

`throw` ends the function it stands in, immediately, and then walks out of
every function that called it. The value it carries out is called an
exception, and it leaves through an emergency exit instead of through
`return`. Put this into `src/index.ts` and reload:

```ts
const half = (value: number): number => {
  if (value < 0) {
    throw new Error(`Cannot halve ${value}`);
  }

  return value / 2;
};

const report = (value: number): void => {
  console.log('report starts');
  console.log(half(value));
  console.log('report ends');
};

report(10);
report(-4);
console.log('the last line of the file');
```

The console:

```
report starts
5
report ends
report starts
Uncaught Error: Cannot halve -4
```

The second `report` printed its first line and then stopped in the middle.
`report ends` never came, and neither did `the last line of the file`, even
though that line sits outside every function. The exception walked out of
`half`, then out of `report`, and the module never got control back either.
That walk is what the stack under the red line lists, innermost first.

Nobody stopped the exception, so the browser did, and printing a red line is
the only move the browser has. Anywhere earlier along the way out, your own
code can step in and say: I know about this one, hand it to me.

## Catching {#sec-exceptions-try}

`try` marks a block of code that might throw, and `catch` marks the block that
runs when it does. Wrap the call inside `report` in one:

```ts
const report = (value: number): void => {
  console.log('report starts');
  try {
    console.log(half(value));
    console.log('still inside try');
  } catch (error) {
    console.log('inside catch', error);
  } finally {
    console.log('inside finally');
  }

  console.log('report ends');
};

report(-4);
console.log('the last line of the file');
```

Reload and read the order:

```
report starts
inside catch Error: Cannot halve -4
inside finally
report ends
the last line of the file
```

`still inside try` is missing, because the `throw` jumped straight from the
middle of `half` into the `catch` block and skipped everything in between.
The four lines after the `catch` all ran, though. Once an exception is caught,
the program is healthy again: `report` finishes, the module runs to its last
line, and nothing red shows up anywhere.

The third block, `finally`, ran after the `catch`. Both exercises below lean
on the precise rule for when `finally` runs, which is the first question in
the research box further down.

## The compiler will not let you read the message {#sec-exceptions-unknown}

The `catch` block received the object that `throw` sent up, and that object has
the message inside it. Try to print just the message:

```ts
  } catch (error) {
    console.log('inside catch', error.message);
  }
```

The line gets a red squiggle, and `npm run verify` spells it out:

```
src/index.ts(15,33): error TS18046: 'error' is of type 'unknown'.
```

`unknown` is TypeScript's way of saying "there is a value here, and I have no
idea what". It has to say that, because `throw` is allowed to send up any
value at all, not only an `Error`. So the compiler hands you the value and
blocks every property until you prove what you are holding.

`instanceof` is the proof. It asks whether an object was built from a given
class:

```ts
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof Error) {
      console.log('inside catch', error.message);
    }
  }
```

Inside that `if`, TypeScript knows `error` is an `Error`, and `error.message`
is the text you passed to `new Error(...)`. An `Error` carries two more
properties next to `message`, and the research box below sends you to look
them up.

## An error class of your own {#sec-exceptions-custom}

`Error` is a class, and a class can be extended. That is how you tell one kind
of problem from another. Create `src/validation-error.ts`:

```ts
export class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ValidationError';
  }
}
```

`super(message)` hands the text up to `Error`, which stores it in `message`
for you. The line after it sets `name`, one of the two properties the research
box asks about.

Now a `catch` block can tell the two apart:

```ts
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof ValidationError) {
    errorParagraph.textContent = error.message;
  } else if (error instanceof Error) {
    errorParagraph.textContent = 'Something went wrong. Look in the console.';
    console.error(error);
  }
}
```

The first branch is for a mistake you expected, so the user reads your message.
The second is for everything else, which means a bug: the user gets a neutral
line and you get the object in the console, where `console.error` marks it as
an error.

The order of the two branches is not free. A `ValidationError` is also an
`Error`, so putting the wide branch first would swallow every validation
message and turn it into `Something went wrong`. Ask for the narrow kind
first, always.

## Who throws, and who catches {#sec-exceptions-where}

A class throws when it cannot keep its own rules. A `Rectangle` with a width of
-5 is not a rectangle, so its constructor refuses to build one. The class has
no idea whether a web page or a test is using it, so it cannot write into a
paragraph. Throwing is how it says no without guessing who is listening.

The user interface catches. Your `index.ts` knows there is a red paragraph on
the page, so it turns the message into something a person reads.

Mistakes you expect from a user often need no throw at all. An empty field in a
form is normal, and an `if` right next to the input handles it in two lines.
Check those where the check is simple, and keep the throw behind them for
everything the check missed.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Never write an empty catch

```ts
} catch {
  // nothing to see here
}
```

A `catch` that does nothing turns a loud failure into silence. The page shows a
stale result and the console stays clean, so the bug waits until someone else
trips over it. When you catch, do something with what you caught: show it, log
it, or hand it on with another `throw`.
:::

::: {.research title="`finally`, and what an `Error` carries"}
Both exercises below need three details this chapter stops at.

1. Your calculator disables a button at the start of a `try` block and gives it
   back in `finally`. Name every way out of a `try` block that still runs the
   `finally` block, and say where you read it.
2. Next to `message`, an `Error` object carries `name` and `stack`. What does
   each of the two hold for a plain `new Error('Something broke')`?
3. `Number('')` and `Number('abc')` do not give you the same thing. What does
   each one return, and which of the two does `Number.isNaN` catch?

Question 3 decides whether your calculator's check works, and the exam runs
without internet, so that one has to stick.
:::

## Exercise A: the calculator, with a model {#sec-exceptions-exercise-calculator}

Your calculator from the chapter on types for elements does its arithmetic
inside the click listener. Now that arithmetic moves into a class of its own
that refuses bad input by throwing, and `index.ts` catches what it throws.

Open your calculator project from `homework/`. If it is not there any more,
build it again: the files below are the ones that chapter shipped, and its
exercise steps say what `src/index.ts` has to do.

{{< exercise calculator >}}

1. Create `src/validation-error.ts` with the `ValidationError` class from this
   chapter.
2. Create `src/calculator.ts` with an exported class `Calculator`. Give it one
   method, `calculate(left: number, right: number, operator: string): number`,
   and move the `switch` over the operator into it. The method returns the
   result and touches no element on the page.
3. Guard the method. When `left` or `right` is `NaN`, throw a
   `ValidationError` with the message `Please type a number into both fields.`.
   When the operator is `/` or `%` and `right` is `0`, throw a
   `ValidationError` with the message `You cannot divide by zero.`, the same
   rule the calculator had before. In the `default` branch of the
   `switch`, throw a plain `Error` that names the operator it does not know.
4. In `src/index.ts`, import both classes and create one `Calculator` above the
   click listener.
5. Rewrite the click listener. Disable the button as its first line. Then open
   a `try` block that reads both fields, converts them with `Number`, calls
   `calculator.calculate(...)`, writes the full line such as `3.5 + 2 = 5.5`
   into the result paragraph, and clears the error paragraph.
6. Put the empty-field check first inside that `try`. When either input
   `value` is the empty string, write `Please fill in both fields.` into the
   error paragraph, clear the result paragraph, and leave the listener with
   `return`.
7. Write the `catch` block with the two branches from this chapter: a
   `ValidationError` puts its own `message` into the error paragraph, any other
   `Error` puts `Something went wrong. Look in the console.` there and goes to
   the console. Clear the result paragraph in both cases.
8. Add the `finally` block that enables the button again.
9. Run `npm start` and try four inputs in a row: `3.5 + 2` gives the result and
   no red text, `10 / 0` gives the divide message, `12abc * 2` gives the number
   message, and an empty first field gives the fill-in message. The button must
   be clickable after every one of them.
10. Break it from the HTML. Add `<option value="^">^</option>` to the
    `<select>` in `index.html`, an operator the calculator never learned,
    pick it, and click Calculate. The page shows
    `Something went wrong. Look in the console.`, and your `default` branch
    is in the console. Remove the option again.
11. Run `npm run verify` and fix what it reports.

## Exercise B: shapes that refuse to be wrong {#sec-exceptions-exercise-shapes}

Open your shapes calculator from the chapter on polymorphism, the project with
`Shape`, `Rectangle`, `Square`, `Ellipse`, `Circle`, and `Line` in six files.
Its five buttons build shapes from random numbers between 1 and 100, so no bad
shape can reach a constructor yet. You change that.

1. Copy `src/validation-error.ts` from your calculator into this project.
2. Guard three constructors. In `Rectangle`, `Ellipse`, and `Line`, right after
   the `super()` call, throw a `ValidationError` when a width, a height, a
   radius, or a length is `0` or below. Write a message that names the shape,
   for example `A rectangle needs a width and a height above 0.`.
3. `Square` and `Circle` get no check of their own. Follow what `new Square(-3)`
   does, step by step, until you see why they do not need one.
4. Give the page a field that can hold a bad number. Above the buttons in
   `index.html`:

   ```html
   <p>
     <label for="sideLength">Side length</label>
     <input id="sideLength" type="number" value="10">
   </p>
   ```

   And under the total line, a place for the message:

   ```html
   <p id="error" class="error"></p>
   ```

   Add `.error { color: firebrick; }` to `src/styles.css`.
5. In `src/index.ts`, fetch `#sideLength` and `#error` the usual way, and add
   both to the `if` that throws when an element is missing.
6. Write a helper next to `render`:

   ```ts
   const showError = (error: unknown): void => {
     // the two branches from this chapter go here
   };
   ```

   In the branch for anything that is not a `ValidationError`, log `error.name`
   next to the error itself, so the console names the kind and shows where it
   came from.
7. Rewrite the listener of `addSquareButton`. Instead of a random number, it
   builds the `Square` from `sideLengthInput.valueAsNumber` inside a `try`
   block that then clears the error paragraph and calls `render`. Catch with
   `showError`.
8. Test it. `12` adds `Square with side 12` and the total grows by 144. `-3`
   puts a red line on the page and leaves the list untouched.
9. Now break a caller on purpose, the way a typo in an id would. Add
   `<button id="breakButton" type="button">Break it</button>` after the five
   shape buttons and fetch it. Its listener opens a `try` block that looks up
   `#thisIdDoesNotExist`, throws
   `new Error('Element #thisIdDoesNotExist not found')` when the lookup gives
   `null`, and builds a `Rectangle` with any two numbers below the check.
   That last line never runs, because the lookup always fails; it is there so
   the listener looks like a real one. Catch with `showError`.
10. Click both buttons and compare. The bad side length puts your own sentence
    on the page. The broken button puts the neutral sentence there and writes
    the name and the stack into the console. That difference is the whole point
    of writing an error class of your own.
11. Run `npm run verify` and fix what it reports.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

The other four buttons still pick numbers between 1 and 100 and can never go
wrong. Change one of them to `Math.floor(Math.random() * 21) - 10`, wrap its
listener in the same `try`/`catch`, and click it 20 times. The model refuses
the sizes below 1 even though no user typed them, which is what the safety net
behind a form is for.
:::
